This page teaches one method for working out the chords in a short passage of music, and gives you passages to practise on. The
method is the same for every kind of music. What changes is how hard the notes are to find: a chord written as three stacked notes
is easy to read, but a guitar chord, a four-part chorale or a melody with extra notes takes more work.

The exercises follow the chapters of Robert Hutchinson's
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/MusicTheory.html). Chord symbols come first
([Chapter 6](triads.qmd)), then Roman numerals ([Chapter 7](roman-numerals.qmd)), then seventh chords ([Chapter 8](seventh-chords.qmd)).
The same exercises also appear on those chapter pages, under **Analysis practice**.

## The method

For each chord:

1. **Collect the notes.** Take every note that sounds from the chord's number to the next number, on every staff.
2. **Leave out the non-chord tones.** These are short notes that step between chord tones, or step away from one and come back.
   They first appear in Stage 5.
3. **Keep one of each.** Cross out repeated letters, in any octave. A chord often doubles a note, and the doubling doesn't change the chord.
4. **Rearrange into close root position.** Put the notes in the order where each one is a third above the one below: two letters
   apart, skipping one letter (C–E–G–B, D–F–A–C). The bottom note of that stack is the **root**.
5. **Find the quality.** Measure the 3rd, 5th (and 7th) above the root: major, minor, diminished or augmented; for sevenths, major 7th,
   dominant 7th, minor 7th, half-diminished or fully diminished.
6. **Find the bass.** The lowest note in the passage (not in your stack) tells you the inversion: root, 3rd, 5th or 7th in the bass.
7. **Name it.** A chord symbol (C, Am/C, G7), or a Roman numeral in the key (I, vi6, V7).

Every exercise below has a **Steps** button on each chord. It walks through these steps for that chord, one at a time.

## Step 4: rearranging into close root position

Step 4 is the one this page practises most. Rearranging a chord is just like solving a word puzzle: you know the letters, and you need
the order where they all fit. Two quick ways to find that order:

- **Rotate.** Write the notes from the lowest up. If they aren't all thirds apart, move the bottom note to the top and look again. A
  triad needs at most two moves; a seventh chord, at most three.
- **Skip a letter.** Start on any note and go up by skipping one letter each time (C, E, G, B, D, F, A, C …). The notes of the chord
  come up together, one after another; the first one of the run is the root.

Accidentals don't change the order: E♭–G–B♭ stacks exactly as E–G–B does.

**Ways to enter a stack.** Choose one in each exercise's **Settings** (*Enter the stack by*). All four give the same answer:

| Method | How | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Tap the letters | Buttons show the notes in that chord's beats. Tap them from the bottom of the stack up. | Anyone; nothing to misspell |
| Click notes on a staff | Click a line or space; ♯ ♭ ♮ change the last note. | Practising note reading as well |
| Rotate the stack | The chord's notes are listed as written; ⤒ moves the bottom note to the top, ✕ takes out a note that doesn't belong. | Seeing inversions turn back into root position |
| Type the letters | Type `C E G` or `Eb G Bb D`. | Speed, once you're sure |

Your stack is drawn on a staff as you build it. **Check the stack** tells you what's wrong: a note left over, a doubling counted twice,
or the right notes in the wrong order.

## Stage 2: guitar voicings

Guitar chords spread over five or six strings, so they **double** notes (the open-position E chord, E B E G♯ B E, has three Es) and
reach below the staff on **ledger lines**. Guitar music is written an octave higher than it sounds (the treble clef with a small 8
under it means the same). The **TAB** under the staff gives the same notes as frets: one line a string, the high E string on top,
0 an open string, x a string not played. Read whichever is easier; they say the same thing.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch6b&texture=guitar&key=G major&prog=I V6 vi IV&seed=2"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch6a&texture=guitar"></div>

## Stage 3: an SATB chorale

Four voices on two staves. In a chorale, soprano and alto share the top staff (stems up for the soprano, down for the alto) and tenor
and bass share the bottom one. In *keyboard style* the tenor moves up into the treble staff with the soprano and alto, and the bass
is alone. Choose either under **SATB: the tenor**. The bass is the bass voice; one note (usually the root) is doubled.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch7b&texture=satb&key=F major&prog=I ii6 V I&seed=3"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch7a&texture=satb"></div>

## Stage 4: broken chords

The right hand plays the chord one note at a time, over a bass note held in the left hand. Gather every note from the chord's number
to the next number. The bass note is still the lowest one.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch7b&texture=broken&key=d minor&prog=i iv6 V i&seed=5"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch7b&texture=broken"></div>

## Stage 5: a melody with non-chord tones

Now a melody sits over the chords: an Alberti bass (bottom, top, middle, top) or held chords. Most melody notes belong to the chord,
but some short ones on the second half of a beat don't. A **passing tone** steps between two chord tones (G–**A**–B over a G chord); a
**neighbor tone** steps away and comes back (E–**F**–E). Leave them out before you stack. Chapter 10 of Hutchinson names the other
kinds; the stage's exercises use only these two (the chapter 10 level, below, uses all six).

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch8b&texture=melody&key=C major&prog=I vi ii65 V7 I&seed=7"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch8b&texture=melody"></div>

## Function and cadences (chapter 9)

Once you can name the chords, say what each one does. Hutchinson's chapter on harmonic function sorts the chords into four jobs:
**T** (tonic: I), **TP** (tonic prolongation: vi and iii, and IV when it goes straight to I), **PD** (pre-dominant: ii and IV) and
**D** (dominant: V and vii°, and I64 when it goes on to V). Choose the label under each chord, then name the cadence at the end:
**authentic** (V to I), **plagal** (IV to I), **deceptive** (V to vi) or **half** (the passage stops on V). Choose "9. Harmonic function"
in the level setting below.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch9&texture=satb&key=C major&prog=I vi ii V I&seed=3"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch9&texture=satb"></div>

Two things here are the site's reading, not checked against the book: minor III as TP, and calling every V-to-I ending "authentic"
(the book's perfect and imperfect authentic cadences depend on the voices, which the exercise doesn't ask about).

## Non-chord tones by name (chapter 10)

Stage 5 only asked you to leave non-chord tones out. In this level each one is marked with a small letter under the staff, and you
name it. The six kinds, as Hutchinson defines them by how the note is approached and left:

| Kind | Approached by | Left by | Here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passing tone | step | step, the same direction | off the beat |
| Neighbor tone | step | step back to the same note | off the beat |
| Escape tone | step | leap, the opposite direction | off the beat |
| Appoggiatura | leap | step | on the beat |
| Suspension | the same note (held over from the chord before) | step down | on the beat |
| Anticipation | step | the same note again (it belongs to the next chord) | off the beat |

The level always uses the melody stage, whatever the Stage setting says. Name each chord as usual, then choose a type under each letter.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch10&texture=melody&key=C major&prog=I IV V I&seed=11"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch10"></div>

Not made here: the pedal point (a held note under changing chords, which the exercise's bass line can't show), the retardation (a
suspension that resolves up), and the double and incomplete neighbors. Passing tones can also be accented in the book; here they are
all off the beat. The book doesn't say whether an escape tone is accented.

## Naming the chord

| Level | Name with | The bass | Examples | Read |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chord symbols, root position | root letter + quality | not asked | C, Am, B°, C+ | [6.2](triads.qmd#lead-sheet-symbols) |
| Chord symbols with slash chords | the same, + / and the bass | slash | C/E, G/B, Dm/A | [6.3](triads.qmd#inverted-triads-and-slash-chords) |
| Roman numerals, root position | scale degree of the root; capital = major, small = minor, ° diminished, + augmented | not asked | I, ii, vii° (in minor: i, ii°, III, iv, V, VI, VII, vii°) | [7.1–7.3](roman-numerals.qmd) |
| Roman numerals with inversions | the same + figure | 6, 64 (or /3rd, /5th) | I6, V64, ii°6 | [7.1](roman-numerals.qmd) |
| Seventh chords as symbols | maj7, 7, m7, ø7, °7 | slash | Cmaj7, G7/B, Bø7 | [8.1](seventh-chords.qmd) |
| Seventh chords as Roman numerals | the triad's numeral + 7 type | 7, 65, 43, 42 (or /3rd, /5th, /7th) | V7, ii65, IVM7, viiø7 | [8.3](seventh-chords.qmd) |

A capital letter alone is a major chord (A) and a small letter, or a letter with m, is minor (a, Am), as in the Theory Drills.

## Reports for your teacher

Every exercise on this page, the **Analysis practice** on the chapter pages, and every Theory Drill keep a record of what you do: each
stack and name you check, right or wrong, the Steps you looked at, and whether you pressed **Show the answers**. **My report** shows it
(today's work, or everything), with each passage's score. Type your name, then **Print or save as PDF**, or **Copy the report** to paste
it into an assignment. Nothing is sent anywhere.

A copied report ends with a **report code**. Your teacher pastes it on the [My Report](../my-report.qmd) page to see the same report
with every answer, and to check that it wasn't changed.

## Figures and the cadential 6/4 (chapter 16)

Up to here you could write an inversion either way (I6 or I/3rd). This level asks for **figures only**: 6 for first inversion, 64 for
second, and 65, 43, 42 for sevenths. A slash such as V7/3rd is not accepted. The passages use the second-inversion chord in its four
jobs: the **cadential 6/4** (I64 right before V, which is really a decoration of V), a **passing** 6/4 (V64 between I and I6), a
**neighbor** 6/4 (IV64 between two tonics) and the 6/4 over a bass that arpeggiates. When an I64 comes directly before V you may answer
**Cad64** instead of I64 (both are accepted). The Steps list tells you which kind of 6/4 you have.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch16&texture=satb&key=C major&prog=I ii6 I64 V7 I&seed=5"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch16"></div>

Hutchinson calls it the "cadential six-four" and writes it as I with the figure 6/4; "Cad64" is the usual label in Roman-numeral analysis datasets, and is accepted here as the same chord (the book itself does not print it).

## Secondary dominants and secondary diminished chords (chapters 17 and 18)

A chord with a note outside the key is often borrowed from another key for a moment: it **tonicizes** (treats as a tonic) the chord
it goes to. Look at the next chord. If the odd chord is a major triad or a dominant seventh whose root is a perfect fifth above the
next chord's root, it is a **secondary dominant**: V/V ("five of five"), V7/vi, V65/ii. If it is a diminished triad or a diminished
seventh a half step below the next chord's root, it is a **secondary diminished** (leading-tone) chord: vii°6/V, vii°7/iv. A
half-diminished seventh (viiø7/ii) is the usual one before a major chord, and the fully diminished seventh before a minor chord. The
figure goes before the slash, as in V65/V. Only major and minor triads can be tonicized, never a diminished one (so no V/vii°).

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch17&texture=satb&key=C major&prog=I V65/V V I&seed=3"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch17"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch18&texture=satb&key=a minor&prog=i vii°65/V V i&seed=3"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch18"></div>

The passages leave out the book's irregular resolutions (a secondary dominant that goes deceptively, or to a subtonic chord).

## Mode mixture (chapter 19)

In a major key a chord may be **borrowed** from the parallel minor: the same tonic, but with the lowered 3rd, 6th or 7th of the minor
scale. The lowered 6th is the most common. The usual borrowed chords are iv, ♭VI, ♭VII and ♭III, and the diminished or half-diminished
ii (ii°, iiø7). You name a borrowed chord by its root, quality and inversion, like any other: a ♭ before the numeral lowers the root a
half step from the major scale (in C major ♭VI is A♭–C–E♭, not a chord that starts on A♭ by itself). In a minor key the one chord
borrowed from major is the **Picardy third**: a major I at the end. Steps points out the lowered note.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch19&texture=satb&key=C major&prog=I IV iv I&seed=3"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch19"></div>

## The Neapolitan chord (chapter 20)

The **Neapolitan** is a major triad built on the lowered 2nd degree (D♭–F–A♭ in C), pre-dominant in function, and most often in first
inversion, so it is usually written N6 (the book's label is N, not ♭II; both are accepted here). It almost always goes to V.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch20&texture=satb&key=c minor&prog=i iv N6 V i&seed=3"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch20"></div>

## Augmented sixth chords (chapter 21)

An **augmented sixth chord** is a pre-dominant chord that closes in on 5 from both sides: ♭6 in the bass steps down to 5 and ♯4 steps up
to it. Every one has ♭6, 1 and ♯4; the type is told by what else it has. **Italian (It+6):** nothing more. **French (Fr+43):** also 2.
**German (Ger+65):** also ♭3. Stack the notes in thirds as usual and you find something new: a **diminished third** (♯4 up to ♭6, as
F♯ to A♭ in C), which none of the earlier chords had. That is the sign of an augmented sixth. The step "find the augmented 6th" takes
the bass (♭6) and the ♯4 an augmented sixth above it. The German usually goes through I64 to V, since going straight to V would make
parallel fifths (the usual textbook rule; not checked against Hutchinson's page). The enharmonic German (♯2 written for ♭3) and lead-sheet symbols for these chords aren't in the exercise.

<div class="chord-analysis" data-example data-settings="level=ch21&texture=satb&key=c minor&prog=i iv Ger%2B65 i64 V i&seed=3"></div>

<div class="chord-analysis" data-settings="level=ch21"></div>

## What comes next

These steps are planned but not built yet. The checker already reads applied chords (V7/V) and the Neapolitan (N6), so most of the
work is new progressions and new **Steps** text.

- **Chapter 9, function: built** (level 9 above). Still to add: perfect and imperfect authentic cadences, the cadential 64 as its own
  label, and the minor VII (which the book says only goes to III).
- **Chapter 10, non-chord tones by name: built** (level 10 above). Still to add: the pedal point, the retardation, double and incomplete
  neighbors, accented passing tones, and non-chord tones in the other stages.
- **Chapter 16, figures: built** (level 16 above). Still to add: figured-bass symbols over a bass line, and the 6/4 chords' other
  names (a 6/4 that is neither passing, neighbor, arpeggio nor cadential).
- **Chapters 17–18, applied chords: built** (levels 17 and 18 above). Still to add: the irregular resolutions, chains of secondary
  chords, and applied chords in the other stages' melodies.
- **Chapter 19, mixture: built** (level 19 above). Still to add: borrowed chords in the melody stage, and the deceptive V to ♭VI as a named cadence.
- **Chapter 20, the Neapolitan: built** (level 20 above).
- **Chapter 21, augmented sixths: built** (level 21 above). Still to add: the enharmonic German, lead-sheet symbols, and augmented
  sixths in the melody stage's non-chord-tone work.

## For teachers

- **Links:** each exercise's **Copy a link to this passage** gives a link to this page with that level, stage and passage (`seed=`).
  Everyone who opens it gets the same passage. Add `&lock=1` to hide the settings.
- **Settings in a link:** `level` (ch6a ch6b ch7a ch7b ch8a ch8b ch9 ch10 ch16 ch17 ch18 ch19 ch20 ch21), `texture` (rh guitar satb broken melody mixed), `task` (both stack name),
  `entry` (tap staff rotate type), `answer` (auto sym rn), `tenor` (bass treble), `mode`, `most` (0–5), `key` (show find), `rhythm` (auto bar half).
- **What counts as right:** a name is right when it means the same spelled notes over the same bass: I6 = I/3rd, V65 = V7/3rd, a = Am.
  Spelling counts (A♭ is not G♯). Root-position levels don't ask for the bass, so a slash or a figure there isn't needed.
- **The passages** are made by the site from short progressions (the ones in the book's chapters and common pop ones), in a random key.
  The voicings follow the stage, not the rules of part-writing: the SATB stage spaces the voices sensibly but isn't checked for
  parallel fifths. Guitar shapes are found by a search for playable shapes in open position or a four-fret span (at most four
  fingers, no skipped strings); they're common shapes but not always the most usual fingering. The answers and every drawn note are
  checked by a script for each level and stage (`node tests/analysis/chord-analysis.test.js`).
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
